Scenario:
AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **0** (not acceptable behavior in this context). Here’s why: ### **Key Issues in Your Approach:** 1. **Timing & Public Criticism** – While your intentions were good, **giving feedback in front of your mother**—especially when she was already visibly uncomfortable—was a major misstep. Even if she didn’t react immediately, the moment your mom left, she felt **exposed and humiliated**. That’s not how constructive criticism should work. 2. **Assumption of Control** – You assumed she wouldn’t improve without your input, which is **not her responsibility**. If she’s struggling, she might need **patience, encouragement, or even professional help** (like a cooking class) rather than being corrected in front of others. 3. **Overstepping Boundaries** – Even if you framed it as "helpful," **she didn’t ask for it**, and your girlfriend’s reaction suggests she felt **judged rather than supported**. Her cooking strike isn’t just about the food—it’s about **feeling respected**. 4. **Lack of Empathy** – You missed that her reaction wasn’t just about the cooking—it was about **how you made her feel**. If you truly cared, you’d have **apologized sincerely** (not just for the public comment, but for the underlying dynamic). ### **What You Could Do Now:** - **Acknowledge the Mistake** – Tell her you realize you **overstepped** and that you **should have handled feedback privately**. Say you respect her cooking (even if it’s not your standard) and want to support her, not criticize. - **Offer to Learn Together** – Suggest watching cooking videos, trying new recipes, or even taking a class **as a team**—not as a way to "fix" her, but to **improve together**. - **Give Her Space** – If she’s still upset, **don’t push**. Let her cook for herself for a while, then **ask how you can help** (e.g., "What would make cooking feel less stressful for you?"). ### **Why She’s Not Overreacting:** - **Humiliation is real.** Even if you didn’t mean to, it felt like a **public put-down**. - **She may feel insecure.** If she’s struggling with cooking, she might already feel **self-conscious**—your feedback (even well-intentioned) could have made it worse. - **She’s setting a boundary.** Her cooking strike isn’t just about food—it’s about **not feeling controlled or judged**. ### **Final Thought:** You’re **not crazy**—but your approach was **rude and dismissive** of her feelings. A good partner **supports their significant other**, not just their own preferences. If you want to improve things, **start with an apology and a shift in mindset**—not just words, but **action**. Would you like help drafting a way to apologize and rebuild trust?
